title: Right-Angled Trigonometry: Sin, Cos and Tan
description: Labelling opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse, the ratios SOHCAHTOA, finding missing sides and angles, angles of elevation and depression, and exact values for IGCSE Maths 0580.

notes.heading: Labelling the Sides: Hypotenuse, Opposite and Adjacent
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Trigonometry compares the **sides** of a right-angled triangle with one of its acute angles. The three sides are named relative to the angle you pick:
• The **hypotenuse** is the side opposite the right angle — always the longest side, and it never changes.
• The **opposite** side is the side facing your chosen angle.
• The **adjacent** side is the remaining side, next to the angle (but not the hypotenuse).

🔑 How it works
Label the angle first, then ask: which side is straight across from it (opposite)? Which side touches it but is not the hypotenuse (adjacent)?

💡 Worked Example
In a triangle right-angled at B, with angle A at the other end of base AB: the hypotenuse is AC, the side opposite angle A is BC, and AB is adjacent to angle A.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping opposite and adjacent. If you relabel the OTHER acute angle, opposite and adjacent swap — the hypotenuse stays the same.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Labelling depends on WHICH angle you are working with.
• The right angle itself is never the labelled angle.

✅ Check
For the same triangle seen from angle C instead of angle A: does BC become the adjacent side?

notes.heading: The Three Ratios: SOHCAHTOA
notes.body:
📌 Definition
For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle:

$$\sin \theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \quad \cos \theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \quad \tan \theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$$

The memory hook is **SOHCAHTOA**: Sin = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cos = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tan = Opposite/Adjacent.

🔑 How it works
Each ratio is a single number fixed by the angle: every right-angled triangle with the same acute angle gives the same ratio, however big the triangle is.

💡 Worked Example
A triangle has opposite $6$ and hypotenuse $10$ for angle $\theta$: $\sin \theta = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using a ratio that divides by zero-length or placing the hypotenuse on the bottom of tan — tan never involves the hypotenuse.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• sin, cos and tan of an angle are RATIOS (pure numbers), not lengths.
• $\sin \theta$ and $\cos \theta$ of an acute angle sit between $0$ and $1$; $\tan \theta$ can exceed $1$.

✅ Check
If adjacent $= 8$ and hypotenuse $= 17$, then $\cos \theta = 8 \div 17 \approx 0.471$.

notes.heading: Choosing the Right Ratio
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Pick the ratio that joins the two sides you care about — ignore the third side entirely:
• opposite and hypotenuse involve $\sin$;
• adjacent and hypotenuse involve $\cos$;
• opposite and adjacent involve $\tan$.

💡 Worked Example 1
You know the angle and the hypotenuse, and want the opposite side: use $\text{opp} = \text{hyp} \times \sin \theta$.

💡 Worked Example 2
You know both shorter sides (opposite and adjacent) and want the angle: use $\tan$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reaching for sin by habit. Read the two sides FIRST, then let the pairing choose the ratio.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Label the triangle from the marked angle before choosing anything.
• One ratio involves each PAIR of sides, so the pairing always decides uniquely.

✅ Check
Angle $50^\circ$, hypotenuse $14$, find the side next to the angle: which ratio uses adjacent and hypotenuse?

notes.heading: Finding a Missing Side
notes.body:
🔑 How it works
Label the sides, choose the ratio, substitute, then multiply or divide:
• Known angle and hypotenuse, want opposite: $x = \text{hyp} \times \sin \theta$.
• Known angle and hypotenuse, want adjacent: $x = \text{hyp} \times \cos \theta$.
• Known angle and adjacent, want opposite: $x = \text{adj} \times \tan \theta$.

💡 Worked Example 1
Hypotenuse $12$, angle $30^\circ$, opposite side $x$: $x = 12 \sin 30^\circ = 12 \times 0.5 = 6$ cm.

💡 Worked Example 2
Hypotenuse $14$, angle $50^\circ$, adjacent side $x$: $x = 14 \cos 50^\circ \approx 9.00$ cm.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Dividing instead of multiplying. With the hypotenuse known and a shorter side wanted, you MULTIPLY by the ratio (a value below 1), so the answer must be smaller than the hypotenuse.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Write the ratio word first (SOH), then put numbers in — it prevents top/bottom slips.
• Estimate sanity: the hypotenuse must stay the longest side.

✅ Check
A ladder problem gives $6 \sin 62^\circ \approx 5.30$ — slightly over half of 6, because $\sin 62^\circ$ is roughly $0.88$.

notes.heading: Finding a Missing Angle
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The inverse ratios work backwards from a ratio to its angle: if $\sin \theta = k$ then $\theta = \sin^{-1} k$ (read as 'sin inverse of k'). Likewise $\cos^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$.

🔑 How it works
1. Form the ratio from the two known sides.
2. Apply the matching inverse on the calculator in **degree mode**.

$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}\right)$$

💡 Worked Example 1
Opposite $7$, hypotenuse $14$: $\sin \theta = 0.5$, so $\theta = \sin^{-1} 0.5 = 30^\circ$.

💡 Worked Example 2
Opposite $4.5$, adjacent $6$: $\tan \theta = 0.75$, so $\theta = \tan^{-1} 0.75 \approx 36.9^\circ$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Calculator in RAD mode: $\sin^{-1} 0.5$ returns $0.524$ (radians) instead of $30^\circ$. Check the mode before every trig calculation.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $\sin^{-1} \theta$ notation means the INVERSE function, not $1/\sin$.
• An answer of $0$ to $90$ degrees in degree mode is plausible for an acute angle.

✅ Check
$\cos^{-1} 0.5 = 60^\circ$ — because $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$.

notes.heading: Angles of Elevation and Depression
notes.body:
📌 Definition
An **angle of elevation** is measured UP from the horizontal line at the observer's eye to look at something higher. An **angle of depression** is measured DOWN from the horizontal to look at something lower.

🔑 How it works
Both angles sit at the horizontal, never at the vertical. Draw a light dashed horizontal through the observer, then put the angle between it and the line of sight. The situation always forms a right-angled triangle:
• looking up from distance $d$ at height $h$: $\tan(\text{elevation}) = h \div d$
• same triangle seen from the object: the angle of depression from the top equals the angle of elevation from the bottom (horizontal lines are parallel, so the angles are alternate).

💡 Worked Example
From flat ground $20$ m from the foot of a vertical tower, the angle of elevation of the top is $35^\circ$: $h = 20 \tan 35^\circ \approx 14.0$ m.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Measuring the depression angle from the vertical cliff or wall instead of the horizontal — that gives the complement of the real angle.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 'Angle of elevation' always means from the horizontal looking up.
• Observer height (eye level) must be ADDED to the triangle's height.

✅ Check
An angle of depression of $18^\circ$ to a boat $25$ m out gives a cliff height $25 \tan 18^\circ \approx 8.12$ m.

notes.heading: Exact Values and the Range of Sin and Cos
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Some angles have exact trig values worth memorising:

$$\sin 0^\circ = 0, \; \sin 30^\circ = 0.5, \; \sin 45^\circ \approx 0.707, \; \sin 60^\circ \approx 0.866, \; \sin 90^\circ = 1$$

$$\cos 0^\circ = 1, \; \cos 30^\circ \approx 0.866, \; \cos 45^\circ \approx 0.707, \; \cos 60^\circ = 0.5, \; \cos 90^\circ = 0$$

$$\tan 0^\circ = 0, \; \tan 30^\circ \approx 0.577, \; \tan 45^\circ = 1, \; \tan 60^\circ \approx 1.732$$

🔑 How it works
As an acute angle grows from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$: $\sin$ rises from $0$ to $1$, $\cos$ falls from $1$ to $0$, and $\tan$ rises from $0$ and grows past $1$ beyond $45^\circ$. Cos takes the mirror image of sin: $\cos \theta = \sin(90^\circ - \theta)$.

💡 Worked Example
Because $\cos \theta = \sin(90^\circ - \theta)$, the value $\cos 63^\circ$ equals $\sin 27^\circ$. Given $\sin 27^\circ = 0.454$, so $\cos 63^\circ = 0.454$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
A screen shows $\sin \theta = 1.4$ and students press on — no angle (acute or otherwise) has sine above $1$, so something is wrong with the triangle labels or the arithmetic.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• For acute angles: $0 < \sin \theta < 1$ and $0 < \cos \theta < 1$; $\tan 45^\circ = 1$ is the crossing point.
• $\sin$ and $\cos$ of complementary angles swap: $\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ$.
• Exact values appear in non-calculator papers — learn the table above.

✅ Check
$\tan 45^\circ = 1$ because the opposite and adjacent sides are equal in a $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle.

flashcards.definition: The side opposite the right angle; the longest side of a right-angled triangle.
flashcards.example: In a triangle right-angled at B, the side AC is the hypotenuse.

flashcards.definition: sin of an angle = opposite divided by hypotenuse.
cos of an angle = adjacent divided by hypotenuse.
tan of an angle = opposite divided by adjacent.
Use the ratio that joins the two sides you know or want: opp-hyp is sin, adj-hyp is cos, opp-adj is tan.
Side = hypotenuse x sin (or cos) of the angle, or adjacent x tan.
Build the ratio, then use the matching inverse function in degree mode.
flashcards.example: sin = 0.5, so the angle is sin^-1(0.5) = 30 deg.

flashcards.definition: Calculator setting so inverse trig returns degrees; rad mode returns numbers like 0.524 instead of 30.
flashcards.example: sin^-1(0.5) = 0.524 means the calculator is in rad mode.

flashcards.definition: Angle measured up from the horizontal at the observer's eye to a higher object.
Angle measured down from the horizontal to a lower object; it equals the matching angle of elevation from the object back to the eye.
flashcards.example: Depression 18 deg from a cliff to a boat 25 m away: height = 25 x tan(18) = 8.12 m.

flashcards.definition: sin 30 = 0.5, sin 45 = 0.707, sin 60 = 0.866, tan 45 = 1, with cos mirroring sin in reverse.
For any angle, sin and cos never exceed 1 in size; tan can. A 'sin' value above 1 signals an error.
flashcards.example: Opposite 8 over hypotenuse 5 is impossible: the opposite side cannot beat the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is
choices: the side next to the right angle
the side opposite the right angle
always the base of the triangle
questions.explanation: The hypotenuse faces the right angle and is always its longest side. It never changes when the acute angles are relabelled.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has an angle $\theta$ with opposite side $6$ cm and hypotenuse $10$ cm. What is $\sin \theta$?
questions.explanation: SOH: sin = opposite/hypotenuse = 6/10 = 0.6. The option 0.8 is cos of the same angle (adjacent 8 over hypotenuse 10).

questions.stem: For an angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle, the adjacent side is $8$ cm and the hypotenuse is $17$ cm. What is $\cos \theta$, correct to 3 decimal places?
questions.explanation: CAH: cos = adjacent/hypotenuse = 8/17 = 0.471. The option 2.125 flips the fraction, and 0.882 is the sine (opposite 15 over hypotenuse 17).

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has an angle $\theta$ with opposite side $5$ cm and adjacent side $12$ cm. What is $\tan \theta$ to 3 decimal places?
questions.explanation: TOA: tan = opposite/adjacent = 5/12 = 0.417. The option 2.400 is the fraction upside down, and 0.385 is sin (5 over the 13 cm hypotenuse).

questions.stem: What is the exact value of $\tan 45^\circ$?
questions.explanation: In a 45-45-90 triangle the opposite and adjacent sides are equal, so tan 45 = 1. It is the crossing point where tan passes through 1.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse $12$ cm and one acute angle of $30^\circ$. What is the length of the side opposite the $30^\circ$ angle?
questions.explanation: Opposite = hypotenuse x sin of the angle = 12 x sin 30 = 12 x 0.5 = 6 cm. The option 10.4 cm is 12 cos 30, the other side.

questions.stem: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is $14$ cm and one acute angle is $50^\circ$. What is the length of the side ADJACENT to the $50^\circ$ angle, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: Adjacent = hypotenuse x cos = 14 x cos 50 = 9.00 cm. The option 10.7 is 14 sin 50, the opposite side, and 16.7 is 14 tan 50.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has an angle $\theta$ with opposite side $7$ cm and hypotenuse $14$ cm. Work out $\theta$.
questions.explanation: sin of the angle = 7/14 = 0.5, so the angle = sin^-1(0.5) = 30 deg. The option 60 deg is the OTHER acute angle of the triangle.

questions.stem: A ramp rises $4.5$ m vertically over a horizontal distance of $6$ m. What angle does the ramp make with the horizontal, to 1 decimal place?
questions.explanation: The rise is opposite and the run is adjacent, so tan of the angle = 4.5/6 = 0.75, giving tan^-1(0.75) = 36.9 deg. The 53.1 deg option is the angle with the vertical.

questions.stem: From a point on level ground $20$ m from the foot of a vertical tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $35^\circ$. How tall is the tower, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: Height is opposite the 35 deg angle and the 20 m ground distance is adjacent, so height = 20 x tan 35 = 14.0 m. The option 11.5 m uses sin, which would be the slant distance, not the height.

questions.stem: From the top of a vertical cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is $18^\circ$. The boat is $25$ m (horizontally) from the foot of the cliff. How high is the cliff, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: The angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the boat, so cliff height = 25 x tan 18 = 8.12 m. The option 7.73 m comes from using sin with the horizontal distance.

questions.stem: An observer whose eye level is $1.5$ m above horizontal ground stands $30$ m from the foot of a vertical flagpole. The angle of elevation of the top of the pole from the observer's eye is $50^\circ$. How tall is the flagpole, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: Height above eye level = 30 x tan 50 = 35.8 m, then ADD the eye level: total = 35.8 + 1.5 = 37.3 m. The option 34.3 m wrongly subtracts the eye level instead of adding it.

questions.stem: Which of these has the greatest value?
questions.explanation: tan 65 is about 2.14: tan exceeds 1 for any angle above 45 deg, while sin and cos stay below 1. The trap option sin 25 actually equals cos 65 (about 0.423), and sin 65 is about 0.906 — both below tan 65.

questions.stem: A ladder $6$ m long leans against a vertical wall. The ladder makes an angle of $62^\circ$ with the horizontal ground. How far up the wall does the ladder reach, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: The wall height is OPPOSITE the 62 deg angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so height = 6 x sin 62 = 5.30 m. The option 2.82 m is 6 cos 62, the distance of the foot from the wall.

questions.stem: Given that $\sin 27^\circ = 0.454$, what is the value of $\cos 63^\circ$?
questions.explanation: Cos is the mirror of sin: cos of an angle equals sin of (90 minus that angle), and 90 - 63 = 27, so cos 63 = sin 27 = 0.454. The option 0.891 is cos 27 itself.
